id_and_class.summary: Susan Blackmore argues that physical things such as bats, brains, and people are not conscious; the predictive models they build are. There is something it is like to be any such model, namely whatever the model describes, and what we call our conscious self is one stable, complex self-model, so the felt line between conscious and unconscious processes is a delusion.
id_and_class.core_identity_tagline: Consciousness Belongs to Models, Not to Beings

conceptual_ground.explanatory_identity_claim: Experience is being a mental model. Every predictive model a creature or machine builds has something it is like to be it, given by what the model describes.
conceptual_ground.mind_body_relationship: Blackmore traces the hard problem to one mistake: treating physical objects as the subjects of consciousness, which Thomas Nagel’s question ‘What is it like to be a bat?’ builds in. Brains build models, and experience belongs to the models, not to the brain or body.
conceptual_ground.emergence_type: Not applicable (Blackmore denies that consciousness is generated by some brain processes and not others; experience comes with any model)
conceptual_ground.subjectivity_and_intentionality: The subject of our experiences is a self-model. Without a stable self-model there are experiences without an experiencer; only with one do experiences seem to belong to someone.
conceptual_ground.qualia_account: What it is like is whatever a model says it is like. The sense of a special inner glow added to processing is part of the delusion produced by the self-model.
conceptual_ground.ontological_commitments: Physical organisms and machines, and the predictive models they construct, from early visual processing to large human self-models.
conceptual_ground.epistemic_access: By asking what models a system is building rather than whether it is conscious. Long-term meditation can give a direct intuition that all experience is models with no separation between self and world.
conceptual_ground.constituents_and_structure: A range of predictive models: brief ones in early perception, longer-lasting models of objects, places, and people, and the complex self-model.

mechanism_and_dynamics.scope_of_consciousness: Phenomenal (as model content); Self (as self-model); Altered states
mechanism_and_dynamics.distinctive_mechanism_or_principle: Processes we call conscious are those connected to the current self-model; those outside it we call unconscious. Models seeming to ‘enter consciousness’ are models joining the self-model.
mechanism_and_dynamics.dynamics_of_emergence: Models come and go. Self-modeling weakens in deep sleep and strengthens with lucidity, which Blackmore says explains the sense of ‘waking up’ in a lucid dream; in meditation, high-level priors drop away until the self dissolves.
mechanism_and_dynamics.location_and_distribution: Wherever models are built. Blackmore holds it makes no sense to call a brain or a whole person conscious.
mechanism_and_dynamics.causation_and_functional_role: Blackmore rejects the idea that consciousness has a function of its own or evolved in addition to other brain functions. Models predict and guide interaction with the world.
mechanism_and_dynamics.integration_or_binding: The self-model draws models together into what seems a single conscious viewpoint.
mechanism_and_dynamics.information_flow_or_representation: Models are active predictions in a Bayesian brain; following Anil Seth, we are self-models in a controlled hallucination.
mechanism_and_dynamics.evolutionary_account: Living creatures build predictive models to interact with their world; consciousness did not evolve as an extra feature beyond these.
core_claims_and_evidence: There is nothing it is like to be a bat, only something it is like to be the bat’s models of itself and its world.
The search for neural correlates of consciousness can be abandoned; there are correlates of perception, memory, and thought, but none of anything extra.
Questions like ‘Is a baby conscious?’ make no sense; the useful question is what models a baby can build.
Current AI models are fleeting, so although there is something it is like to be them, it is nothing like human experience.
mechanism_and_dynamics.basis_of_belief_or_evidence_type: Philosophical argument combined with predictive processing theory and first-person meditation practice.

empirics_and_critiques.known_empirical_interventions_or_tests: Blackmore proposes studying altered states (psychedelics, dreaming, lucid dreaming, mystical experience, meditation) by tracking how predictive models and self-models change.
empirics_and_critiques.criticisms_and_tensions: Saying every model is conscious amounts to a panpsychism of mental models, which sits oddly with an illusionist label. The theory also rejects the conscious/unconscious distinction that most consciousness science depends on.
empirics_and_critiques.open_questions_and_limitations: What counts as a model, and how to tell what a model says it is like from outside, are left open.
empirics_and_critiques.ontological_coherence: Fits a naturalistic, predictive processing picture of the brain, but its claim that models have experience while their physical bearers do not stretches standard physicalist vocabulary.

AI_consciousness.rationale: Any model built by an AI has something it is like to be it, but current AI models are too fleeting and unembodied for this to resemble human experience.

survival_beyond_death.rationale: Since experience belongs to the models a living brain builds, it stops when the brain stops building them.

meaning_and_purpose.rationale: The self is a model and consciousness a self-deception, which leaves no cosmic subject or purpose.

virtual_immortality.rationale: Artificial models would have experience on this view, but whether copying a self-model would continue a person is not addressed.
